title: WOULD YOU STILL FOLLOW JESUS IF OBEYING HIM DESTROYED THE LIFE YOU WORKED SO HARD TO BUILD?
paragraphs: WOULD YOU STILL FOLLOW JESUS IF OBEYING HIM DESTROYED THE LIFE YOU WORKED SO HARD TO BUILD?
When your reputation is on trial, your career is at risk, and the people you love begin walking away, will Jesus still be enough?
There is a version of Christianity that almost everyone is comfortable with.

The kind that gives you peace when life becomes overwhelming. The kind that promises hope when everything falls apart. The kind that fills a church with beautiful songs, encouraging messages, and people who smile when they say, “God is good.”
And God is good.
But there is a question that rarely gets asked when the worship music is playing and everything in your life seems to be going well.
What happens when following Jesus becomes the very reason your life starts falling apart?
Not because you committed a crime.
Not because you were dishonest.
Not because you mistreated somebody.
But because you refused to compromise what you believe Christ has commanded.
Imagine walking into work tomorrow and discovering that the position you spent ten years building is suddenly in jeopardy because you would not participate in something you believe is wrong.
Imagine sitting across from your closest friend, someone who knows your childhood, your secrets, your failures, and your dreams, only to hear the words:
“I don't think we can be friends anymore if you're going to keep believing that.”
Imagine the people who once respected you now whispering about you.
Your name becomes a conversation you were never invited into.
Your intentions are questioned.
Your faith is mocked.
And suddenly, the Jesus you once followed so comfortably is asking you to remain faithful when faithfulness may cost you something you cannot easily replace.
Would you still follow Him?
Don't answer too quickly.
Peter once believed he knew the answer.
And before the rooster crowed, he discovered something terrifying about his own heart.

Jesus had warned His disciples that a night of unimaginable testing was approaching. Peter, full of confidence and sincere devotion, declared that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
He meant it.
That is what makes the story so painful.

Peter was not necessarily pretending when he promised loyalty. He loved Jesus. He had left his fishing nets. He had witnessed miracles. He had walked on water toward Christ. He had heard words that changed his understanding of eternity.
But loving Jesus when you are surrounded by miracles is not the same experience as confessing Jesus when you are surrounded by people who might punish you for it.
Later that night, Jesus was arrested.
The crowds were no longer celebrating Him.
The religious authorities were accusing Him.
His disciples were scattering.
And Peter found himself standing near a fire, trying to stay warm while the world he understood was collapsing.
Then someone recognized him.
“You also were with Jesus.”
Peter denied it.
Another person confronted him.
He denied it again.
Then came the third accusation.
And Peter denied knowing the Lord he had promised never to abandon.
The rooster crowed.
Luke records one of the most devastating details in the entire account:
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Read that slowly.
Jesus looked at Peter.
The One who had called him.
The One who had believed in what grace could make of him.
The One who had washed the feet of men who were about to fail Him.
And Peter remembered.
Scripture says he went outside and wept bitterly.
Sometimes the most painful moment of your spiritual life is not when other people discover your weakness.
It is when you discover it yourself.
When you realize that the approval of strangers has been controlling you more than the Word of God.
When you remember the conversation where you should have spoken truth with love, but chose silence because you were afraid of being disliked.
When you recognize that you have been carefully managing your Christian identity so that it never interferes with your popularity, ambitions, or relationships.
And suddenly Peter's story stops feeling like ancient history.
It starts feeling like a mirror.
Perhaps you have never denied Jesus aloud.
But have you ever hidden your faith because you were embarrassed?
Have you ever laughed at something you knew dishonored God because everyone around you was laughing?
Have you ever allowed people to assume you agreed with something you knew was wrong because correcting them might damage your reputation?
Have you ever been more afraid of losing someone's approval than of disobeying the Savior who died for you?
These questions are not meant to convince you that Christ has stopped loving you.
They are meant to expose the places where fear has been quietly discipling your heart.
Because there is a difference between having faith in Jesus and allowing Jesus to rule the decisions that frighten you.
And the Gospel does not leave us comfortable with that difference.
Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
The Greek text uses the expression ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ καθ’ ἡμέραν (aratō ton stauron autou kath’ hēmeran).
It means, in context, “let him take up his cross daily.”
That word καθ’ ἡμέραν — kath’ hēmeran — matters.
Daily.
Not merely during an emotional altar call.
Not only when the church is singing your favorite worship song.
Not only when obedience brings encouragement, promotion, or applause.
Daily.
In the ordinary moments when following Christ demands a decision nobody else may ever see.
For the first-century audience, a cross was not a decorative symbol or an inspiring metaphor for minor inconvenience. Crucifixion was a brutal Roman instrument of execution and public humiliation.
When Jesus spoke about carrying a cross, He was calling His followers to a kind of allegiance that could involve shame, suffering, and even death.
He was not promising that every Christian would lose a career, be rejected by family, or face execution.
He was teaching that no earthly security could be treated as more ultimate than loyalty to Him.
And that distinction matters.
Because Christianity is not a command to chase suffering.
It is a call to follow Christ faithfully, even when suffering comes because of that faithfulness.
There are Christians who mistake being disliked for being persecuted.
There are people who speak cruelly, behave arrogantly, refuse correction, and then claim that everyone opposing them must be opposing Jesus.
But Scripture does not permit that confusion.
Peter himself later wrote:
“But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters.” — 1 Peter 4:15, KJV
Not every consequence is persecution.
Not every disagreement is hatred.
Not every closed door is evidence that you stood for righteousness.
Sometimes we need repentance, humility, wisdom, or accountability.
But there are also moments when you can act with genuine kindness, honesty, and integrity, and still face rejection because your allegiance to Christ is unwelcome.
And when that moment comes, the question becomes deeply personal.
Whose approval has the final authority over your life?
There was another man who faced that question long before Peter.
His name was Daniel.
He was not an irresponsible rebel trying to create controversy. Scripture presents him as an exceptionally capable administrator whose enemies struggled to find legitimate grounds for accusation.
Daniel 6:4 describes their inability to find corruption or negligence in him.
Think about that.
His enemies could not easily attack his professional integrity.
So they attacked his devotion to God.
A royal decree was arranged that would make prayer to anyone other than the king unlawful for thirty days.
Daniel knew about the decree.
He knew the consequences.
He knew that continuing his established practice of prayer could lead to death.
And Daniel 6:10 tells us that he went home and prayed as he had done previously.
No dramatic performance.
No desperate attempt to impress a crowd.
No need to turn his obedience into a spectacle.
Just a man who refused to allow the threat of punishment to become more authoritative than his God.
Daniel did not suddenly become faithful when the lions appeared.
His courage in public was rooted in devotion already practiced in private.
That should make us think.
Because many of us want the courage of Daniel in a crisis while neglecting the daily communion with God that shaped his life.
We want to stand strong when everything is threatened, but we struggle to open our Bibles when nothing is at stake.
We want fearless faith in the workplace, yet sometimes cannot bring ourselves to pray when nobody is watching.
And still, the Lord calls us closer.
Not so we can manufacture heroic personalities.
But so our roots in Christ can grow deeper than our fear of people.
Now imagine a different kind of loss.
Not the loss of a job.
The loss of a friendship.
Someone you love begins to distance themselves because you have decided to follow Jesus seriously.
Perhaps they misunderstand your changed priorities.
Perhaps they feel judged, even when you have not condemned them.
Perhaps they are uncomfortable because the things you once celebrated together are no longer things you can participate in with a clear conscience.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you still love them.
You still remember the laughter.
The late-night conversations.
The years when they were the first person you called after receiving good news.
You do not want to lose them.
You do not want to become cold, superior, or self-righteous.
You just cannot pretend that meeting Jesus has left your life unchanged.
There is a particular kind of grief that comes from being misunderstood by someone whose opinion once meant everything to you.
You rehearse conversations in your head.
You wonder whether you should have explained yourself differently.
You stare at old messages.
You pray for reconciliation.
And somewhere inside, a dangerous temptation begins whispering:
“Wouldn't life be easier if you just stopped taking your faith so seriously?”
This is where discipleship becomes costly.
But remember something essential.
Jesus never commanded you to stop loving people who disagree with you.
He commanded you to love even your enemies.
He never instructed His followers to become unnecessarily offensive.
He called them to truth, mercy, humility, and faithfulness.
Romans 12:18 says:
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
That means you do not need to manufacture conflict to prove you belong to Christ.
You can apologize when you are wrong.
You can listen when someone is hurting.
You can honor a friend without agreeing with every belief they hold.
You can remain gentle when others become harsh.
And you can refuse to compromise your convictions without treating another human being as your enemy.
Because the goal is not to win an argument and lose your witness.
The goal is to remain faithful to Jesus while reflecting His character.
But what if you do everything you reasonably can to preserve peace, and they still walk away?
Then you grieve.
You pray.
You entrust them to God.
And you remember that even perfect love does not guarantee universal acceptance.
Jesus Himself was rejected.
John 1:11 says:
“He came unto his own, and his own received him not.”
The sinless Son of God entered the world He created, and many refused to receive Him.
His rejection was not proof that He lacked love.
His suffering was not evidence that He had lost the Father's purpose.
And His crucifixion was not the end of His story.
But before we reach the empty tomb, we need to look at the cross.
Because the cross reveals something about reputation that we often overlook.
Jesus did not merely suffer physical pain.
He endured public humiliation.
He was falsely accused.
He was mocked.
He was stripped and crucified.
The One who deserved worship was treated as though He deserved contempt.
And Hebrews 12:2 says that He endured the cross, “despising the shame.”
The Greek word αἰσχύνης (aischynēs) refers to shame or disgrace.
The passage does not mean that Jesus enjoyed humiliation or considered suffering insignificant.
It means that the shame associated with crucifixion did not turn Him away from completing His mission.
He endured because of the joy set before Him.
And the outcome was not defeat.
It was redemption.
Now consider the contrast.
We sometimes struggle to confess Christ because we fear being embarrassed.
Yet Christ willingly endured public disgrace to save sinners who could never save themselves.
He did not go to the cross because we had impressive reputations.
He went because we needed mercy.
He did not wait until we became socially acceptable, morally flawless, or spiritually successful.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had repaired everything.
Not after we had become worthy of applause.
Not after we had successfully hidden every scandal.
While we were still sinners.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ, the righteous Son of God, died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He did not come merely to improve our public image.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to forgive sin.
He came to break the power of condemnation.
He came to make dead hearts alive.
And this is why the Gospel is far greater than a message about becoming brave enough to defend your beliefs.
It is the announcement that Jesus has accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
Our courage does not purchase salvation.
Our suffering does not earn forgiveness.
Our willingness to lose friends does not make God indebted to us.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the grace that saves us also begins transforming how we live.
That is where Peter's story becomes extraordinary.
Because the man who denied Jesus beside a fire was not abandoned by the risen Christ.
After the resurrection, John 21 describes Jesus meeting His disciples by the Sea of Tiberias.
There was a charcoal fire.
There was breakfast.
And there was Peter.

The Gospel of John uses the Greek word ἀνθρακιά (anthrakia) for a charcoal fire in John 18:18, where Peter warmed himself during the night of his denial, and again in John 21:9, where the risen Jesus had prepared breakfast.
That repeated detail is striking.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us that the charcoal fire was intended to remind Peter of his failure.
But the narrative places his denial and restoration in scenes with a memorable shared detail.
And what happens beside that second fire is one of the most tender moments in Scripture.
Jesus asks Peter:
“Lovest thou me?”
He asks again.
And again.
Three questions.
Three opportunities for Peter to confess his love.

Many readers notice the Greek verbs ἀγαπάω (agapaō) and φιλέω (phileō) in this exchange. Some interpretations make a sharp distinction between them, but John's Gospel often uses these verbs with overlapping meanings. The safest emphasis is not a speculative hierarchy of different kinds of love, but the unmistakable restoration of a disciple who had failed.
Jesus commissions Peter to care for His sheep.
The man who denied knowing Christ is called to serve Christ's people.
Do you understand what that means for someone who has been living under the weight of shame?
Peter's failure was real.
His denial was serious.
His tears were not meaningless.
But his worst night was not the final chapter of his life.
Jesus did not pretend the denial never happened.
He met Peter in the aftermath of it.
And restored him.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Not an excuse to continue denying Christ whenever life becomes uncomfortable.
Grace is the undeserved mercy of God that forgives, restores, and calls us into a new way of living.
Peter would later stand before religious authorities with a boldness that contrasted dramatically with his earlier fear.
In Acts 4:19–20, Peter and John refuse to stop speaking about what they had seen and heard.
In Acts 5:29, Peter and the other apostles declare:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.”
The frightened disciple had become a courageous witness.
Not because Peter had finally discovered that he was naturally invincible.
But because the risen Christ had restored him, and the Holy Spirit had empowered the apostles for witness.
The transformation was not Peter becoming impressed with himself.
It was Peter becoming increasingly anchored in Jesus.
And perhaps that is the transformation you need today.
Not a louder personality.
Not an aggressive religious identity.
Not the ability to win every theological debate on social media.
But a heart so rooted in Christ that the fear of losing human approval no longer controls your obedience.
Maybe you are reading this while facing a decision at work.
You have been asked to lie, falsify something, betray a confidence, or participate in conduct you know is dishonest.
And you are afraid that doing the right thing will cost you an opportunity you desperately need.
You have bills.
You have family responsibilities.
You have dreams you have worked hard to achieve.
The consequences are not imaginary.
And faithfulness does not mean you must act recklessly or refuse wise counsel.
Seek understanding. Examine the facts. Know your responsibilities. Consider lawful and ethical options. Speak with humility and clarity.
But do not sell your conscience simply because dishonesty has been made convenient.
Proverbs 29:25 warns:
“The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.”
The Hebrew expression חֶרְדַּת אָדָם (ḥerdat adam) speaks of the fear or trembling associated with human beings.
The word translated “snare,” מוֹקֵשׁ (moqesh), evokes a trap.
What a picture.
The fear of people can become a trap.
You begin by wanting to be liked.
Then you become afraid to disappoint.
Then you become afraid to disagree.
Then you become afraid to obey God whenever obedience threatens the image you have carefully constructed.
Eventually, the people whose approval you wanted are controlling decisions that should have been surrendered to the Lord.
And the frightening part is that this captivity can look like success.
You can have the title.
The salary.
The followers.
The connections.
The applause.
And still be terrified of what will happen if people discover that Jesus truly has authority over your life.
What good is a reputation that requires you to betray your convictions to maintain it?
What good is popularity if you are constantly afraid of telling the truth?
What good is being celebrated by everyone if you are becoming a stranger to the person God is calling you to be?
Jesus asked a question that reaches beyond every career and social circle:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — Mark 8:36, KJV

In Greek, the word ψυχή (psychē), translated here as “soul,” can refer to one's life or self. In this passage, Jesus confronts the tragedy of gaining what the world offers while forfeiting one's very life before God.
He is not teaching that money, employment, friendship, or reputation are inherently evil.
He is exposing the terrible exchange that happens when temporary gain becomes more precious to us than following Him.
And some of us are closer to making that exchange than we want to admit.
Not through one dramatic declaration.
But through a thousand small compromises.
One dishonest answer.
One hidden conviction.
One relationship we refuse to surrender to God's wisdom.
One opportunity that demands we silence our conscience.
One more day of saying, “Lord, I'll obey You when it becomes easier.”
But what if easier never comes?
What if the next step of obedience requires trust before the outcome becomes visible?
Would Christ still be worthy?
This is where we must resist turning the Christian life into a bargain.
We cannot say, “Jesus, I will follow You if You guarantee that my reputation will recover.”
Or, “Lord, I will stand for truth if You promise that my career will improve.”
Or, “God, I will obey if You make sure none of my friends leave.”
Jesus has not promised that every faithful believer will enjoy social acceptance or professional advancement.
In fact, 2 Timothy 3:12 warns that those who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will experience persecution.
Yet Scripture also teaches that not every hardship comes from persecution, and that suffering is not always a sign of spiritual maturity.
Our confidence must rest in something deeper than favorable circumstances.
It must rest in Christ Himself.
The One who was crucified is risen.
The One who was rejected is Lord.
The One who calls us to follow Him is the One who promises to be with His disciples.
And when you belong to Him, the verdict of the crowd is no longer the ultimate verdict over your life.
That does not make rejection painless.
It does not make unemployment easy.
It does not remove the ache of an empty chair where a friend once sat.
But it gives suffering a different horizon.
Your life is not ultimately held together by how many people admire you.
It is held in the hands of the Savior who loved you and gave Himself for you.
And now I want to speak to the person who already failed this test.
The person who stayed silent.
The person who compromised.
The person who denied their faith because they were frightened.
The person who has been carrying the memory of that moment for months, perhaps years.
You know exactly what happened.
You remember the room.
The conversation.
The decision.
You remember the uncomfortable feeling afterward.
You told yourself it was not a big deal.
But something inside you knew.
And now every time you read about Peter, you feel the sting.
Please hear this.
Peter's story does not end with the rooster.
And if you turn to Jesus in repentance and faith, your story does not have to end with your failure either.
Do not hide behind excuses.
Do not rename compromise as wisdom simply because the truth hurts.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Make amends where appropriate.
Seek forgiveness from those you have wronged.
And return to Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The promise rests on God's faithfulness and justice, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You do not need to pretend you were courageous when you were afraid.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony.
You can tell the truth.
“I was afraid, Lord.”
“I cared too much about what people thought.”
“I compromised.”
“I put my security above obedience.”
“Please forgive me.”
That kind of honesty is not the death of faith.
It can be the beginning of genuine repentance and renewed obedience.
And perhaps the most important question today is not whether you would have stood beside Daniel or remained faithful beside Peter.
Perhaps it is this:
Will you follow Jesus in the next decision that actually belongs to you?
Will you tell the truth when a lie would be easier?
Will you refuse cruelty even when cruelty would make you popular?
Will you forgive when bitterness would feel more satisfying?
Will you remain faithful to biblical conviction without becoming proud or hateful?
Will you love people who reject your beliefs?
Will you choose obedience when nobody is watching?
Will you keep trusting Christ if the answer to your prayer is not the answer you wanted?
These are not imaginary questions.
They are the places where discipleship enters ordinary life.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to make Christians feel superior to a world that desperately needs the mercy of God.
But to keep pointing wounded, weary, tempted, struggling, and searching people back to Jesus Christ.
Because there are people who wake up every morning fighting battles they do not know how to explain.
People who are surrounded by friends but spiritually lonely.
People who have been attending church for years while secretly drifting away from God.
People who are ashamed of their past.
People who want to understand Scripture but do not know where to begin.
People who need someone to remind them that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and Jesus still transforms lives.
Some of those people may be in your family.
Some may be your closest friends.
Some may be people who have never stepped inside a church.
And one of them might be reading these words right now.
That is why sharing biblical truth matters.
Or, if you are struggling and need prayer, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to explain private details publicly.
But your honest response may help another person realize they are not the only one wrestling with fear, shame, or spiritual exhaustion.
Not to glorify suffering.
Not to glorify yourself.
But to testify to the sustaining grace of Christ.
Someone needs to know that faithfulness is possible.
Someone needs to know that a Christian can lose human approval without losing the love of God.
Someone needs to know that failure does not have to become permanent spiritual defeat.
And someone desperately needs to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
You never know who among your friends is silently asking whether Jesus is worth following when life becomes difficult.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Jesus, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Not merely to read another article.
But to help sustain and expand the work of sharing the Gospel and equipping people to follow Christ.
These resources are meant to help people open the Scriptures, examine their lives honestly, strengthen their understanding of the faith, and continue growing in grace.
And that work needs faithful people who believe it is worth supporting.
It is not a purchase of spiritual blessings.
It is not a requirement for being a faithful Christian.
And it should never replace your responsibility to care for your family, fulfill your obligations, or support your local church.
But it can be a meaningful expression of voluntary Christian generosity, helping sustain the resources and outreach of this ministry.
The New Testament teaches that believers may support those who labor in sharing the Gospel.
Paul wrote:
“Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.” — 1 Corinthians 9:14, KJV
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from a willing heart, not from pressure or compulsion.
That is the spirit of this invitation.
You can still pray.
You can still share Scripture.
You can still encourage someone who is struggling.
You can still help another person encounter the message of Jesus.
The value of your faith is not measured by the amount of money you give.
The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is the message.
More people opening Scripture.
More believers growing in understanding.
More wounded hearts hearing about the mercy of Jesus.
More people discovering that they do not have to remain prisoners of the sins and failures that once defined them.
That simple act can help bring the message into the life of someone we may never reach otherwise.
A person who has been silently compromising their faith.
A person who feels ashamed after denying Christ.
A person who is about to make a decision that could change the direction of their life.
A person who has mistaken their failures for the end of their story.
Because the message they need is not that strong Christians never fall.
It is that Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior who forgives repentant sinners, restores the fallen, and empowers His people to walk in obedience.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought us here.
Would you still follow Jesus if it cost you your reputation?
What if it cost you the promotion?
What if it cost you the invitation?
What if the people who once applauded you began mocking you?
What if someone you deeply loved decided that your faith had become too uncomfortable for them?
Would Jesus still be enough?
Maybe you cannot confidently say yes.
Maybe the question frightens you.
Maybe you recognize more of Peter in yourself than you expected.
Then do not pretend.
Bring that fear to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Ask Him for a heart that loves Him more deeply.
Ask for wisdom to distinguish genuine obedience from unnecessary conflict.
Ask for courage without arrogance.
Conviction without cruelty.
Humility without cowardice.
Love without compromise.
And when the next difficult moment comes, remember that you are not called to face it in your own strength.
Jesus said:
“Without me ye can do nothing.” — John 15:5, KJV
That is not merely a warning about human weakness.
It is an invitation to abide in the One who gives life.
The same Jesus who called Peter out of the fishing boat restored him after his denial.
The same Jesus who suffered public shame was raised in glory.
The same Jesus who calls His followers to take up their cross has already accomplished the work of redemption that no human courage could achieve.
So if your reputation trembles, cling to Christ.
If your career becomes uncertain, seek wisdom and remain faithful.
If your friends misunderstand you, continue to love them.
If you fall, repent and return.
And if the world asks you to trade your Savior for its approval, remember what the cross has already revealed.
You were loved by Christ before the crowd ever knew your name.
You were offered mercy when you had nothing impressive to bring.
And no amount of human applause can replace the grace of the One who died and rose again for sinners.
Perhaps you came into this article asking whether you are strong enough to stand for Jesus.
But the deeper question is whether you are learning to depend on the Savior who can sustain you when your own strength fails.
Peter discovered that his confidence in himself was not enough.
He also discovered that his failure was not greater than the mercy of the risen Christ.
And that is where hope begins.
Not in your perfect reputation.
Not in your flawless courage.
Not in your ability to control what others think of you.
But in Jesus.
The One who sees the truth about you and still calls you to repentance, faith, and new life.
So follow Him.
When people understand.
When they misunderstand.
When obedience is celebrated.
When obedience is costly.
And when you stumble, do not run farther into hiding.
Run back to the Savior.
Because the world may remember the night Peter denied Jesus.
But the Gospel also remembers the morning Jesus restored him.
The crowd may remember the moment you fell, but Jesus can write a future that your failure never had the power to erase.
